newsitem.title: UK: Coffee nations may try to cool prices.
newsitem.headline: Coffee nations may try to cool prices.

text.p: Coffee-producing nations may suspend export quotas to try to cool an explosive rally that has lifted benchmark U.S. coffee bean futures to a 20-year high when they meet in London this week.

As roasters (processors) in the United States and Europe pass on a soaring world price at the shops, some of the 14 members of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) worry that people will switch to tea or soft drinks instead.
Producers must show "we are not a cartel", says Paian Nainggolan of Indonesia, whose output is exceeded only by Brazil and Colombia.
Coffee is on its longest unbroken rally for two decades.
A volatile mix of factors -- low stocks, tight supply from Colombia and fears that Brazil may have another frost -- has lured speculators to the futures markets that set benchmark world prices.
Last week saw New York spot May futures for quality arabica beans trade at $2.79 per pound, the highest since June 1977.
July, the most active and representative contract, has more than doubled to reach $2.62 this year. Prices eased slightly at week's end on profit taking, dealers reported.
The ACPC accounts for 76 percent of world output and will assess implementing its 1996/97 (July/June) export programme when it meets in London on Monday and Wednesday.

Rules now in force aim to cap exports at 25.5 million bags in the first half of 1997. But at talks in March the members rescinded new cuts by 500,000 bags as the market tightened, and some delegates now talk of suspending quotas altogether.
A top official from Colombia hinted last week that he would be ready to put any extension of the export curbs on hold.

"The producers' desire is to send a signal to the markets and there's no question of having prices at a certain level just for the sake of it or of creating artificial conditions," said Jorge Cardenas, veteran head of the Colombian Coffee Federation.
He could have support from Central American producers such as Costa Rica, Honduras, Venezuela and El Salvador.
Government officials say linchpin Brazil's position will only be defined during the London talks, but indications are that it will back a continuation of some form of programme.
Gilson Ximenes, the president of the growers' Brazilian Coffee Council, said he was in favour of the current policy.
Brazil is expected to exceed its quota for January-June by about 1.0 million bags but local exporters say there was a shortfall of 2.0 million in quotas in the previous programme.
Delegates from Indonesia and Ivory Coast, producing the less-prized robusta beans, said they had open minds.
Ivory Coast Commodities Minister Guy-Alain Gauze, who pushed for big export cuts in January, agrees that there are now supply problems.
Traders say governments will be under pressure to ease curbs from growers eager to cash in on high prices.

The French and British were on Friday the latest among consumers to be stung by new price rises in the shops. Douwe Egberts France, owned by Sara Lee Corp, said this year's French retail increases on its arabica coffees now totalled around 45 percent.
French Cafes Excella SA said it planned new retail prices rises in June. But marketing director Jean-Jacques Dothee said he did not believe that futures reflected supply/demand fundamentals.
"There is no risk of a coffee shortage. We are being held hostage by a speculative game..." he said.
Dothee also gave a warning that high prices might scare away consumers, notably young people switching to soft drinks.
In 1994-95 French roasters passed on the cost of higher futures and consumption fell by seven percent. It rebounded by three percent in 1996 when prices went down, he said.
